endorsements.quote: An AI model card for the lay public, similar to a nutrition label on food, can be posted in patient portals or clinician tools to improve transparency without requiring technical literacy.

Patients, who want greater clinical oversight of medical AI, and clinicians who want greater protection from liability from erroneous medical AI, will both have greater trust in medical AI if clinicians can be formally trained in how to use AI, when to trust AI, and when not to automatically trust AI.

Characteristics of patient data used in a diabetes AI model are available, including age of onset of diabetes, BMI, laboratory data (e.g., HbA1c, antibody status), diabetes education, technology use, etc.
Data for an algorithm must derive from multiple patient groups to include populations that have been under-represented
The system must be validated for specific subgroups within a disease, e.g., type 1 vs. type 2 vs. gestational diabetes
An inclusive community program for all community stakeholders from the very beginning of developing an AI program
AI systems should support and enhance – not replace - human decision-making

unlisted_practices: Share model code and validation datasets in AI publications to allow others to reproduce results.
Share large diverse datasets, taking privacy and security into account, to enable fair head-to-head model comparisons.
Run parallel multicenter reproducibility testing of AI tools at independent clinics using local or shared synthetic datasets, and publish performance summaries.
Publish a public trust scorecard showing accuracy versus clinician benchmarks, training data diversity, date of last independent audit, and known limitations.
Implement two-tier human review in which high-confidence AI recommendations are logged for audit and low-confidence or novel cases are flagged for clinician review.
Perform ongoing post-market monitoring of AI performance drift and recalibrate models when needed.
Adopt cybersecurity standards such as IEEE 2621 for AI-enabled diabetes devices.
Provide plain-language explanations of AI privacy and security practices to patients.
Establish clear frameworks for apportioning liability for AI-generated recommendations among clinicians, healthcare organizations, and developers.
Co-design patient education materials on AI with patient advocacy groups and clinicians.
Provide patients with plain-language summaries of AI decisions and visual dashboards showing trends.
Provide clinician AI literacy and data interpretation education programs.
Use consensus-building multidisciplinary panels so clinicians can negotiate workflow adaptations and liability issues.
Provide patient-facing AI outputs in culturally resonant formats and local languages, accounting for health and digital literacy.
Establish an ongoing feedback mechanism and community focus groups for AI fairness.
Validate AI models with independent registries and test across diverse institutions and populations.
Evaluate AI accuracy using randomized controlled trials and real-world evidence studies.
Assess AI datasets using a reference population score to measure diversity of training, validation, and testing data.
Adopt mature AI governance structures in health systems.

screen.reason: This is an editorial/commentary that provides recommendations and framework priorities for achieving trustworthy medical AI (focusing on diabetes care) across six key attributes.
